title: core.tool.config — the exact configuration a tool ran with
description: The second half of Gregor's order of 2026-08-08: embed the tools' CODE **and their configurations**. A core.tool node carries the code; this carries the settings one RUN of it used. They are separate nodes because they have different lifetimes — one tool is run twenty times with twenty configurations, and duplicating the source twenty times to record that would be absurd — and because a configuration is the thing most likely to be edited and re-recorded later, which law 6's append-only versions handle cleanly for a node of its own. The `params` object is the tool's OWN key names, verbatim, unrenamed and unvalidated by werk: a format that normalised a tool's parameter names would be recording what it wished the tool had been passed. Narrative spec: spec/SPEC.md section 3.17.

config_id.description: Stable kebab-case id for this configuration.

tool_node.description: node_id, IN THIS PACKAGE, of the core.tool this configures. An internal reference — hermetic by construction (law 1). A config whose tool is not in the package is a promise about another file; where the tool genuinely is not carried, use `external_tool` instead and accept that the record is weaker.

external_tool.description: For the honest case where the configuration is known and the tool is not carried: a hosted API, a 12 GB checkpoint's sampler, a licensed binary that may not be redistributed. Recording the configuration is still worth doing; pretending the tool is present is not.

why_not_embedded.description: Say it plainly: 'hosted API', 'proprietary', '12 GB of weights'. An absent reason reads as an oversight.

params.description: Every parameter the caller actually passed, under the caller's OWN key names. Not normalised, not renamed, not reordered by werk. This is the same rule core.recipe's step.params states and it is the rule that makes the record re-runnable rather than merely descriptive.

params_provenance.description: The same three-way distinction core.recipe makes about prompts, applied to configuration, because it is the same lie waiting to happen. `recorded`: the running tool persisted this exact object at run time. `reconstructed`: it did not, and the object was rebuilt from the tool's own source or its defaults — legitimate, common, and NOT the same claim, so `reconstruction` is then mandatory. `authored-after`: a human wrote down what they believe the settings were, and it must never be presented as the first.

source_file.description: Path INSIDE this package of the source the values were read out of — normally the core.tool's entrypoint.

how.description: One sentence: 'the module-level defaults, none of which the invocation overrode'.

config_files.description: Configuration that is itself a FILE the tool loaded — a YAML, a ComfyUI workflow, a shader define block — carried verbatim so it can be fed back in. Byte-for-byte, never reserialised: a config round-tripped through a JSON parser is a config whose key order and number formatting have quietly changed.

verbatim.description: true when these bytes are exactly what the tool read. false, with a note, when they were regenerated.

environment.description: The facts about the machine that a re-run is sensitive to. Deliberately short: this is not a system inventory, it is the four or five things that actually change a result.

library_versions.description: name -> version, for the libraries whose arithmetic the output depends on.

determinism.description: The same three grades core.recipe uses, applied to one tool run: `deterministic` promises the same bytes out for the same bytes in with this configuration; `stochastic` means a random source is not pinned; `descriptive` means a re-run cannot be expected to reproduce the output at all. When present, `determinism_note` MUST say which specific fact puts it in that grade.

unrecorded.description: Facts about this run that were NOT captured and cannot be recovered. The same idea core.recipe's mandatory `unrecorded[]` carries: it is what lets a reader tell a complete record from a merely confident one.
